title: The Differences Between AI, ML, and DL
body: AI, ML, and DL are often used interchangeably, but their scopes differ. AI is a broad field that enables computers to perform tasks that humans do intelligently.
when_to_show: When reviewing ai, ml, deep_learning, model
detail: ML is a method of learning rules from data, and DL is one of the machine learning methods that uses multi-layer neural networks. LLMs are also deep learning-based models. When you come across the term “AI” while reading code, you should check the context to determine whether it actually refers to a rule-based program, a machine learning model, or a deep learning model. This card is not intended merely for memorizing word definitions; it serves as a supplementary explanation to help you identify how these concepts relate to variables, data types, functions, files, and API flows in actual Python code.

title: LLM: Large Language Model
body: LLM stands for Large Language Model.
detail: These models are trained on vast amounts of text to understand and generate sentences, and are used for tasks such as question-answering, summarization, translation, and code generation. However, since LLMs do not always guarantee factual accuracy, it may be necessary to search for and verify sources. When reading code, LLM calls must be understood in the context of prompt construction, input tokens, output processing, cost, and error handling.

title: MLM: Masked Language Model
body: MLM stands for Masked Language Model, a training method in which parts of a sentence are masked and the model is trained to fill in the blanks. For example, the model can be asked to predict the blank in the sentence “Python is a [MASK] language.” It has been widely used in BERT-family models and is closely related to sentence understanding and representation learning. Since its training method may differ from that of generative models, when reading code, you should distinguish MLM from methods that continuously generate the next word. This card is not intended merely for memorizing word definitions; rather, it serves as a supplementary explanation to help you understand how these concepts relate to variables, data types, functions, files, and API flows in actual Python code. The MLM approach can be understood as a training method where part of a sentence is masked, and the user must predict the word that should fill that blank. Since its purpose differs from that of general conversational generative models, when reading code, you must distinguish whether it is intended for blank-filling prediction or sentence generation. Even if language model names are similar, their training methods and intended uses may differ.
detail: MLM can be understood as a learning method where part of a sentence is masked and the user must fill in the blank. It differs in approach and purpose from conversational generative models, which continue writing the next sentence. When reading the code, you should verify whether the model is being used for blank prediction, sentence classification, embedding generation, or free generation. In particular, it is helpful to distinguish between the BERT family and generative LLMs.

title: Token: A segment read by the model
body: A token is the basic unit that a model uses to read and process text.
detail: Even if something looks like a single word to a human, it can be split into multiple tokens internally by the model, and Korean characters or special characters can also affect the number of tokens. Since the model has a limit on the number of tokens it can process at once, long documents or conversations must be split into smaller chunks. When reading code, settings such as `token limit`, `context window`, and `max_tokens` are linked to computational cost, response length, and the likelihood of failure.

title: Embedding: Converting Meaning into Numeric Vectors
body: Embedding is a method of converting the meaning of sentences or words into numerical vectors.
when_to_show: When reviewing embedding, vector, rag, search
detail: Since computers cannot directly understand the meaning of text, they transform it so that sentences with similar meanings are positioned close to each other in the numerical space. The vectors created in this way can be used for search, recommendation, clustering, and duplicate detection. In RAG, the question and document fragments are embedded, and then the closest match is found. When reading code, embedding is the step of converting text into a searchable numerical representation.

title: Vector DB: A database for embedding search
body: A vector database is a database designed for embedding-based search. It converts documents or sentences into numerical vectors for storage, and after converting the user’s query into a vector as well, it finds document fragments with similar meanings. While traditional keyword search requires exact matches to find results, vector search can find results even if the phrasing differs slightly, as long as the meaning is similar. In RAG, it is frequently used to find relevant evidence and pass it to the model. When reading the code, you should examine the workflow of embedding generation, storage, and top-k search together. This card is not intended merely for memorizing word definitions; it serves as a supplementary explanation to help you understand how these concepts relate to specific variables, data types, functions, files, and API flows in actual Python code. Vector DB code typically converts documents into embeddings and stores them, then searches for items whose embeddings are similar to a query. When reading the code, you should check whether the storage and search phases are separated and what the top-k criteria are.
when_to_show: When reviewing vector_db, embedding, rag, search
detail: A vector database can be viewed as a storage system for search that stores embeddings and finds nearby vectors. When reviewing the code, verify that the document storage phase and the query search phase are separated. The top-k count, filter conditions, similarity criteria, and source metadata directly affect answer quality. You should also check whether the search results are verified rather than simply accepted at face value.

title: RAG: Search and Answer
body: RAG stands for Retrieval-Augmented Generation, a method of generating answers based on retrieved evidence.
when_to_show: When reviewing rag, retrieval, embedding, llm
detail: Rather than answering solely from memory, the model first locates relevant document fragments and then references that content to formulate its response. As such, it is linked to stages such as document retrieval, chunking, embedding, prompting, and citation. When reading RAG code, you should check how the question is converted into a search query, which documents are selected, and how the selected evidence is incorporated into the response.

title: AI Agent: AI That Uses Tools to Achieve Its Goals
body: An AI agent refers to an AI architecture that selects tools and performs multiple steps to achieve a goal. While a simple chatbot focuses on answering questions directly, an agent can use tools such as searching, reading files, performing calculations, and executing code to carry out tasks. However, using tools isn’t always safe, so planning, execution, verification, and constraints are necessary. When reading code, an agent must determine which tools to call, when to call them, and how to verify the results. This card is not intended merely for memorizing definitions; it serves as a supplementary guide to help you identify how variables, data types, functions, files, and API flows are connected in actual Python code. When reviewing AI Agent code, you should not just look at the model’s responses; you must also examine the entire workflow—from defining the goal, to selecting tools, to verifying the execution results. Tool calls—such as searches, reading files, or executing code—may occur in between. When reading the code, you should verify under what conditions the model uses these tools and whether it validates the results of those tools.
when_to_show: Code Agent, Automation, and Tool Usage Issues
detail: An AI Agent is a framework in which a model selects tools and executes a series of steps to achieve a goal. When reviewing the code, don’t just look at the model’s responses; examine the entire workflow—including planning, invoking tools, verifying results, retrying, and handling failures. Using tools doesn’t always guarantee safety, so permission restrictions and verification steps are also necessary.

title: Tool Calling: How the Model Calls Tools
body: Tool Calling is a method in which a model calls upon necessary tools to continue its work. Rather than generating all answers on its own, the model can utilize external functions such as search tools, calculation tools, file-reading tools, and code-execution tools. For example, if a user asks for the latest information, the model uses a search tool; if numerical calculations are needed, it uses a calculation tool. When reading code, you must verify under what conditions the model calls which tools and how it incorporates the results of those tools back into its response. This card is not just for memorizing definitions; it serves as a supplementary explanation to help you identify how these concepts relate to variables, data types, functions, files, and API flows in actual Python code. When solving problems, first locate the line of code where this concept appears, and then determine whether that line reads input, modifies values, evaluates conditions, or stores or outputs results. Tool Calling is a method in which a model retrieves results by calling an external tool, rather than performing calculations or searches directly. When reading the code, you should check the tool’s input schema, call conditions, result validation, and failure handling flow.
when_to_show: When reviewing tool_calling, agent, api, workflow
detail: Tool Calling is a method by which a model invokes an external function in a specified format. When reading the code, check the tool name, input schema, invocation conditions, handling of return values, and the fallback flow in case of failure. You must distinguish whether the content is the model’s direct response or reflects the results of a search or computational tool.

title: Labeling and Annotation
body: Labeling and annotation involve attaching correct answers or descriptive tags to data.
when_to_show: When reviewing labeling, annotation, dataset, training
detail: For example, indicating whether a sentence is positive or negative, marking the location of objects in an image, or assigning difficulty levels and concepts to problem cards are all forms of labeling. AI models are trained or evaluated based on these labels. In code, they may appear as fields such as `label`, `annotation`, `target`, or `answer`. Good labeling significantly influences both model quality and validation quality.

title: Evaluation Sets and Benchmarks
body: Evaluation datasets and benchmarks are reference data used to compare the performance of AI systems or programs. Just because a model produces plausible answers doesn’t necessarily mean it’s good; its performance must be verified against defined problems, correct answers, or evaluation criteria. Even in learning apps, verification criteria such as the number of cards, whether correct answers are included, missing fields, and difficulty distribution are necessary. When reading code, think of `eval` or `benchmark` as procedures to verify whether the results can be trusted. These cards are not just for memorizing word definitions; they serve as supplementary explanations to help you understand how variables, data types, functions, files, and API flows are connected in actual Python code. When solving problems, first locate the line in the code where the concept appears, then categorize that line as a step that reads input, modifies values, evaluates conditions, or stores or outputs results. An evaluation set is a set of reference data used to verify whether a model or rule actually works well. Even if the benchmark score looks good at first glance, it’s difficult to guarantee quality if it doesn’t match the specific context in which you intend to use it. When reading code, if you encounter “eval,” you should also check the input data, the criteria for correct answers, the scoring method, and whether failure cases are logged.
when_to_show: When reviewing eval, benchmark, dataset, quality
detail: Evaluation sets and benchmarks serve as criteria for verifying whether a model or rule actually works well. When reading code, I look at the input data, the ground truth, how scores are calculated, and whether failure cases are recorded. A high score alone isn’t enough; I also need to verify that the evaluation data aligns with the context in which I intend to use it.

title: Understanding LLM/API Costs
summary: The cost of the LLM API increases based on the number of requests, input length, output length, and the number of retries.
detail: In batch jobs or AI API calls, the number of requests, input length, output length, and number of retries are all tied to costs. Therefore, you should skip results that have already been processed, use caching, set timeouts and retry limits, and log request and response sizes. During code reviews, we first look for infinite loops, duplicate calls, exposed API keys, and excessive retry attempts following failures.
body: An understanding of LLM/API costs is essential basic knowledge when turning code into a service. While Python tutorials typically start with `print` statements and functions, real-world AI apps can incur costs with every model call. If an external API is called every time a user asks a question, the cost increases based on the number of requests, the number of characters in the input, and the number of characters in the output. Therefore, it’s important to have a structure that caches answers instead of generating the same response from scratch each time, summarizes long documents first, and calls the model only when absolutely necessary. This card helps students understand that it’s not simply a matter of “AI providing an answer,” but that there are costs and limitations associated with running the code. In real-world code, to reduce costs, you should condense inputs, avoid duplicate requests, and limit the number of retries in case of failure. It’s also linked to security, since if an API key is exposed, others could call the model at your expense. Later, when you encounter terms like “rate limit,” “cache,” “batch,” or “token,” think back to this card. When reviewing this card, don’t just memorize the definitions of the terms; also check which variables, functions, and data types they correspond to in actual code. The goal is to apply the concepts you’ve learned from small examples to data processing and service architecture in real-world projects.

title: Retrieval
summary: Retrieval is the stage in which documents or chunk candidates relevant to the query are first identified.
detail: In RAG, the model does not provide an answer immediately; instead, it first searches for relevant evidence. Searches can be performed using keywords, BM25, embedding/vector search, hybrid search, and other methods. During the code review, we examine the workflow involving query input, index search, top_k, score, and reranking.
body: Retrieval is the process by which the system first locates the necessary data before the model generates an answer. When a user asks a question, instead of reading the entire document, the system searches for relevant excerpts and passes them to the model. This allows the model to respond based on actual data rather than relying solely on its memory. In Python code, this corresponds to the process of selecting values that meet certain criteria from a list, finding specific lines in a file, or retrieving relevant documents from a database. When studying retrieval, it is important to distinguish what is being searched for, where the search is conducted, and how the results are incorporated into the response. If there are too many search results, irrelevant content may be mixed in; if there are too few, the evidence needed for the answer may be missing. This practice forms the foundation for understanding RAG, search indexes, vector search, and evidence-based responses. When reviewing this card, don’t just memorize the definitions of the terms; also verify which variables, functions, and data types they correspond to in actual code. title: State estimation
summary: State estimation is the process of using observations to estimate unobservable states such as position, velocity, and attitude.
detail: In robotics, autonomous driving, and UAM, it is difficult to determine the current state immediately because sensor measurements are noisy. Methods such as the Kalman Filter combine predicted values and measured values to produce more stable state estimates. During a code review, look for the `state`, `predict`, `update`, and `noise` variables first.
body: State estimation is the process of estimating the current state of a system. A state is a value that indicates the current condition of a program or device, such as position, velocity, direction, remaining battery life, or progress stage. Since sensor readings are not always perfect, the system calculates the current state by combining the previous state with new observations. For example, if a sensor indicates that a robot has moved a short distance, the system can estimate its new position by adding the distance traveled to its previous position. In Python, variables are linked to code that continuously updates them within loops. Practicing to read the flow of how new values are derived from previous ones—as seen in cumulative variables like `total`, `count`, and `last`—is the starting point for understanding state estimation. When reviewing this card, don’t just memorize the definitions of the terms; also check which variables, functions, and data types they correspond to in actual code. The goal is to apply the flow you’ve observed in small examples to data processing and service architecture in real-world projects. State estimation is the process of estimating the current state—which is not directly observable—based on multiple observations. It can be viewed as a process that aims to calculate a more plausible state even when sensor values fluctuate or some observations are missing. When reading code, it’s easier to understand if you break it down into input observations, the previous state, update rules, and the final estimated value.

title: Sensor fusion
summary: Sensor fusion is the process of combining data from multiple sensors to achieve more reliable recognition.
detail: For example, LiDAR, radar, cameras, and GNSS/IMU each have their own strengths and weaknesses. Sensor fusion code aligns measurement values with a common state or coordinate system and uses both predicted and observed values together. During a code review, we examine the measurement, timestamp, calibration, and update step.
body: Sensor fusion is a method of combining information from multiple sensors to make more reliable decisions. In robots and autonomous driving systems, cameras, LiDAR, radar, and location sensors each provide different types of information. Cameras are good at detecting color and shape, while radar is effective at providing distance and speed information. Since relying on a single sensor can lead to errors due to light, rain, obstructions, or noise, multiple values are compared together. In Python programming, you can see this concept applied in code that gathers values from multiple variables or lists and uses them to evaluate conditions. The key is to follow how each input is interpreted, the criteria used to combine them, and how the combined result leads to a specific decision. This concept reappears later when reading code involving averaging, filtering, conditional statements, and state estimation.
